readings.c3s3:
¶
'''usurpatory''' (ū-zėr′pa-tō-ri), ''a.'' [< LL. ''usurpatorius'', of or pertaining to a usurper, < ''usurpator'', a usurper, < L. ''usurpare'', pp. ''usurpatus'', usurp: see ''usurp''.] Characterized or marked by usurpation; usurping.

'''usurpatrix''' (ū′zėr-pā-triks), ''n.'' [= F. ''usurpatrice'', < LL. ''usurpatrix'', fem. of ''usurpator'', a usurper: see ''usurpatory''.] A woman who usurps. ''Cotgrave.''

'''usurpature''' (ụ̄-zėr′pạ-t̮ūr), ''n.'' [< L. ''usurpare'', pp. ''usurpatus'', usurp, + ''-ure''.] The act of usurping; usurpation. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus, lit and launched, up and up roared and soared
A rocket, till the key o’ the vault was reached,
And wide heaven held, a breathless minute-space,
In brilliant ''usurpature''.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 306.}}}}

'''usurpedly''' (ū-zėr′ped-li), ''adv.'' By an act or acts of usurpation; in a manner characterized by usurpation. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They temerariously and ''usurpedly'' take on themselves to be parcel of the body. ''Hallam'', Const. Hist., III.}}

'''usurper''' (ū-zėr′pėr), ''n.'' [< ''usurp'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who usurps; one who seizes power or property without right: as, the ''usurper'' of a throne, of power, or of the rights of a patron.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou false ''vsurper'' of Gods regal throne.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 35.}}
Sole heir to the ''usurper'' Capet. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 78.}}

'''usurping''' (ū-zėr′ping), ''p. a.'' Characterized by usurpation.
{{smaller block|The worst of tyrants an ''usurping'' crowd. ''Pope.''}}

'''usurpingly''' (ụ̄-zėr′ping-li), ''adv.'' In a usurping manner; by usurpation; without just right or claim. ''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 13.

'''usufruct''' (ū′zụ̄-frukt), ''n.'' [= F ''usufrug'' = Sp. Pg. ''usufructo'' = ''usofrutto'', < L. ''usus fructus'' (abl. and orig., two words, ''usus fructus, usus et fructus'', the use and enjoyment: ''usus'', use; ''fructus'', enjoyment, fruit: see ''use''<sup>1</sup> and ''fruit''.] In ''law'', the right of enjoying all the advantages derivable from the use of something which belongs to another so far as is compatible with the substance of the thing not being destroyed or injured. {{smaller|''Quasi-usufruct'' was admitted in the civil law in the case of certain perishable things. In these cases an equivalent in kind and quantity was admitted to represent the things destroyed or injured by use. (''Amos.'') ''Usufruct'' is often used as implying that the right is held for life, as distinguished from more limited and from permanent rights.}}
{{smaller block|In the rich man’s houses and pictures, his parks and gardens, I have a temporary ''usufruct'' at least.
{{right|''Lamb'', Bachelor’s Complaint.}}}}

'''usufruct''' (ū′zū-frukt), ''v. t.'' [< ''usufruct'', ''n.''] To hold in usufruct; subject to a right of enjoyment of its advantages by one while owned by another.
{{smaller block|The cautio usufructuaria that property ''usufructed'' should revert unimpaired to the owner on the expiry of the usufructuary’s life interest. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XX. 709.}}}}

'''usufructuary''' (ū-zū-fruk′t̮ū-ā-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= F. ''usufruitier'' = Sp. Pg. ''usufructuario'' = It. ''usufruttuario'', < LL. ''usufructuarius'', one who has the use and profit of, but not the title to (a thing), < L. ''ususfructus'', use and enjoyment: see ''usufruct''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or relating to usufruct; of the nature of a usufruct. ''Coleridge.''

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''usufructuaries'' (-riz). A person who has the usufruct or use and enjoyment of property for a time without having the title. ''Ayliffe'', Parergon. {{smaller block|I have been ever your man, and counted myself but an ''usufructuary'' of myself, the property being yours.
{{right|''Bacon'', Letter, March 25, 1621.}}}}

'''usurarious†''' (ū-zụ̄-rā′ri-us), ''a.'' [< L. ''usurarius'', of usury: see ''usurary''.] Usurious. ''Jer. Taylor'', Rule of Conscience, i. 5.

'''usurary†''' (ū′zụ̄-rạ̄-ri), ''a.'' [= F. ''usuraire'' = Pr. ''usurari'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''usurario'', < L. ''usurarius'', of or pertaining to interest or usury, < ''usura'', usury: see ''usure'', ''usury''.] Usurious. ''Bp. Hall'', Works, VII. 373.

'''usure†''' (ū′zụ̄r), ''n.'' [< ME. ''usure'', < OF. (and F.) ''usure'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''usura'', < L. ''usura'', use, employment, interest, < ''uti'', pp. ''usus'', use: see ''use''<sup>1</sup>.] Interest; usury. ''Chaucer'', Friar’s Tale, l. 9.

{{smaller block|What is ''vsure'', but venyme of patrymonye, and a lawfulle thefe that tellyth ys entent?
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 32.}}}}

'''usure†''' (ū′zụ̄r), ''v. i.'' [< ''usure'', ''n.''] To practise usury.

<poem>I turn no monies in the public bank,
Nor ''usure'' private.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, i. 1.}}}}

'''usurer''' (ū′zụ̄-rėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''usurer'', < OF. (also F.) ''usurier'' = Sp. ''usurero'' = Pg. ''usureiro'' = It. ''usuriere'', < ML. ''usurarius'', a usurer, < L. ''usurarius'', pertaining to use or interest, < ''usura'', use, interest: see ''usure'', ''usury''.] '''1†.''' One who lent money and took interest for it.

{{smaller block|The seconde buffet be-tokeneth the riche ''vserer'' that deliteth in his richesse and goth s[c]ornynge his pore nyghebours that be nedy whan thei come to hym ought for to borough.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 434.}}}}

{{smaller block|Henry, duke of Guise, . . . was the greatest ''usurer'' in France, because he had turned all his estate into obligations.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, i. 87.}}}}
'''2.''' One who lends money at an exorbitant rate of interest; a money-lender who exacts excessive or inordinate interest. See ''usury''.

'''usuring†''' (ū′zṳ̄-ring), ''a.'' [< ''usure'' + ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>.] Practising usury; usurious.
{{smaller block|I do not love the ''usuring'' Jew so well.
{{right|''Fletcher and Shirley'', Night-Walker, iv. 6.}}}}

'''usurious''' (ū-zū′ri-us), ''a.'' [< ''usury'' + ''-ous''.] '''1.''' Practising usury; specifically, taking exorbitant interest for the use of money.
{{smaller block|<poem>Plead not: ''usurious'' nature will have all,
As well the int’rest as the principal.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iii. 15.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining to or of the nature of usury; acquired by usury.
{{smaller block|Enemies to interest, . . . holding any increase of money to be indefensibly ''usurious''. ''Blackstone'', Com., II. 30.}}

'''usuriously''' (ū-zū′ri-us-li), ''adv.'' In a usurious manner.

'''usuriousness''' (ū-zū′ri-us-nes), ''n.'' The character of being usurious.

'''usurous†''', ''a.'' Same as ''usurious''. ''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, v. 4.

'''usurp''' (ū-zėrp′), ''v.'' [< F. ''usurper'' = Sp. Pg. ''usurpar'' = It. ''usurpare'', < L. ''usurpare'', make use of, use, assume, take possession of, usurp, perhaps orig. ''usu rapere'', seize to (one’s own) use: ''usu'', abl. of ''usus'', use; ''rapere'', seize: see ''use''<sup>1</sup> and ''rap''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To seize and hold possession of, as of some important or dignified place, office, power, or property, by force or without right; seize, appropriate, or assume illegally or wrongfully: as, to ''usurp'' a throne; to ''usurp'' the prerogatives of the crown; to ''usurp'' power.
{{smaller block|<poem>That hellish monster, damnd hypocrisie, . . .
''Vsurps'' my place & titles soveraigntie.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 140.}}
<poem>Thou dost here ''usurp''
The name thou owest not.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 453.}}
<poem>White is there ''usurped'' for her brow.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, iii. 1.}}
<poem>Trade’s unfeeling train
''Usurp'' the land, and dispossess the swain.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 64.}}}}
'''2.''' To assume, in a wider sense; put on; sometimes, to counterfeit.
{{smaller block|<poem>O, if in black my lady’s brows be deck’d,
It mourns that painting and ''usurping'' hair
Should ravish doters with a false aspect.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iv. 3. 259.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be or act as a usurper; hence, to commit illegal seizure; encroach: with ''on'' or ''upon''.
{{smaller block|Y<sup>e</sup> Pequents . . . ''usurped upon'' them, and drive them from thence. {{right|''Bradford'', Plymouth Plantation, p. 311.}}
This tendency in political journals to ''usurp upon'' the practice of books, and to mould the style of writers.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, i.}}}}

'''usurpant†''' (ū-zėr′pant), ''a.'' [< L. ''usurpan''(''t''-)''s'', ppr. of ''usurpare'', usurp: see ''usurp''.] Inclined or apt to usurp; guilty of usurping; encroaching. ''Bp. Gauden'', Tears of the Church, p. 473.

'''usurpation''' (ū-zėr-pā′shọn), ''n.'' [< F. ''usurpation'' = Sp. ''usurpacion'' = Pg. ''usurpação'' = It. ''usurpazione'', < L. ''usurpatio''(''n''-), a using, an appropriation, < ''usurpare'', use, usurp: see ''usurp''.] '''1.''' The act of usurping; the act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the place, power, functions, or property of another without right; especially, the wrongful occupation of a throne: as, the ''usurpation'' of supreme power.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''usurpation''
Of thy unnatural uncle, English John.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 9.}}
The Parlament therefore without any ''usurpation'' hath had it alwaies in thir power to limit and confine the exorbitancie of Kings. {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xi.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''law'': (''a'') Intrusion into an office or assumption of a franchise, whether on account of vacancy or by ousting the incumbent, without any color of title. (''b'') Such intrusion or assumption without lawful title. (''c'') The absolute ouster and dispossession of the patron of a church by presenting a clerk to a vacant benefice, who is thereupon admitted and instituted; intrusion.—'''3†.''' Use; usage. [A Latinism.]
{{smaller block|There can be no kind of certainty in any such observations of the articles, because the Greeks promiscuously often use them or omit them, without any reason of their ''usurpation'' or omission.
{{right|''Bp. Pearson'', Exposition of the Creed, ii.}}}}

'''usurpatory''' (ū-zėr′pa-tō-ri), ''a.'' [< LL. ''usurpatorius'', of or pertaining to a usurper, < ''usurpator'', a usurper, < L. ''usurpare'', pp. ''usurpatus'', usurp: see ''usurp''.] Characterized or marked by usurpation; usurping.

'''usurpatrix''' (ū′zėr-pā-triks), ''n.'' [= F. ''usurpatrice'', < LL. ''usurpatrix'', fem. of ''usurpator'', a usurper: see ''usurpatory''.] A woman who usurps. ''Cotgrave.''

'''usurpature''' (ụ̄-zėr′pạ-t̮ūr), ''n.'' [< L. ''usurpare'', pp. ''usurpatus'', usurp, + ''-ure''.] The act of usurping; usurpation. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus, lit and launched, up and up roared and soared
A rocket, till the key o’ the vault was reached,
And wide heaven held, a breathless minute-space,
In brilliant ''usurpature''.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 306.}}}}

'''usurpedly''' (ū-zėr′ped-li), ''adv.'' By an act or acts of usurpation; in a manner characterized by usurpation. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They temerariously and ''usurpedly'' take on themselves to be parcel of the body. ''Hallam'', Const. Hist., III.}}

'''usurper''' (ū-zėr′pėr), ''n.'' [< ''usurp'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who usurps; one who seizes power or property without right: as, the ''usurper'' of a throne, of power, or of the rights of a patron.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou false ''vsurper'' of Gods regal throne.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 35.}}
Sole heir to the ''usurper'' Capet. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 78.}}

'''usurping''' (ū-zėr′ping), ''p. a.'' Characterized by usurpation.
{{smaller block|The worst of tyrants an ''usurping'' crowd. ''Pope.''}}

'''usurpingly''' (ụ̄-zėr′ping-li), ''adv.'' In a usurping manner; by usurpation; without just right or claim. ''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 13.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
